metadata.title: Diminishable Parameterized Problems and Strict Polynomial Kernelization

nodes.name: Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A strict kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le k + c$, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that $L$ admits a strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if~$f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: A kernelization whose output parameter exceeds the input parameter by at most an additive constant.
nodes.origin_citation: Abu-Khzam & Fernau 2006; Chen, Flum, and Müller 2011

nodes.name: Parameter Diminisher
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameter diminisher} for a parameterized problem~$L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps instances~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ to instances~$(x', k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$ and $k' < k$.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time self-reduction that outputs an equivalent instance with strictly smaller parameter.
differentia: $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$ and $k' < k$

nodes.name: Parameter-Non-Increasing Reduction
nodes.statement: Given two parameterized problems~$L$ with parameter~$k$ and~$L'$ with parameter~$k'$, a \emph{parameter-non-increasing reduction} from~$L$ to~$L'$ is an algorithm that maps each instance $(x,k)$ of $L$ to an equivalent instance~$(x',k')$ of~$L'$ in time polynomial in $|x|+k$ such that $k'\leq k$.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time reduction between parameterized problems that never increases the parameter.
nodes.genus: algorithm that maps each instance $(x,k)$ of $L$ to an equivalent instance~$(x',k')$ of~$L'$
differentia: in time polynomial in $|x|+k$ such that $k'\leq k$

nodes.name: Parameter-Decreasing Branching Rule
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameter-decreasing branching rule} for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs a sequence of instances $(y_1,k'),\ldots,(y_t,k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that~$(x,k) \in L \iff (y_i,k') \in L$ for some $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and $k' < k$.
nodes.statement_short: Branching that replaces an instance by several instances of strictly smaller parameter, preserving the answer disjunctively.
differentia: $(x,k) \in L \iff (y_i,k') \in L$ for some $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and $k' < k$

nodes.name: Strict Composition
nodes.statement: A \emph{strict composition} for a parameterized problem $L$ is an algorithm that receives as input $t$ instances $(x_1,k),\ldots,(x_t,k)\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, and outputs in polynomial~time a single instance $(y,k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(y,k') \in L \iff (x_i,k) \in L$ for some $i \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and \item $k' \leq k + c$ for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum}
nodes.statement_short: An OR-composition of $t$ same-parameter instances into one, raising the parameter by at most an additive constant.

nodes.name: Non-Uniform Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A non-uniform strict kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a \emph{non-uniform} polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance~$(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le k + c$, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that $L$ admits a non-uniform strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if $f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: The strict-kernel notion where the kernelization may be computed by a non-uniform polynomial-time algorithm.

nodes.name: Semi-Strict Kernel
nodes.statement: A \emph{semi-strict kernelization} for a parameterized problem~$L$~is a polynomial-time algorithm that on input instance $(x,k)\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ outputs an instance~$(x',k')\in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$, the \emph{semi-strict kernel}, satisfying: \begin{inparaenum}[(i)] \item $(x, k) \in L \iff (x', k') \in L$, \item $|x'| \le f(k)$, for some function $f$, and \item $k' \le c\cdot k $, for some constant $c$. \end{inparaenum} We say that~$L$~admits a semi-strict \emph{polynomial} kernelization if $f(k)\in k^{O(1)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Relaxation of strict kernelization allowing a multiplicative, rather than additive, constant increase of the parameter.

nodes.name: Strong Parameter Diminisher
nodes.statement: A \emph{strong parameter diminisher} for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps instances $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ to instances~$(x', k') \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ such that $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$, and $k' \le k/c$, for some constant $c>1$.
nodes.statement_short: A diminisher that divides the parameter by a constant factor rather than merely decrementing it.
differentia: $(x, k) \in L \text{ if and only if } (x', k') \in L$

nodes.name: Diminishable Problem
nodes.statement: We call a parameterized problem~$L$~\emph{diminishable} if there is a parameter diminisher for $L$.
differentia: there is a parameter diminisher for $L$

nodes.name: Cutwidth
nodes.statement: A graph~$G=(V,E)$ has \emph{cutwidth} at most~$k$ if and only if there exists a linear ordering (layout) $\pi: V \to \{1,\ldots,|V|\}$ of~$G$ where for each real number $1<\alpha<|V|$ we have that for the \emph{cut} at $\alpha$, defined as~$E_{\pi,\alpha}:=\{ \{u,v\} \in E: \pi(u) < \alpha < \pi(v)\}$, it holds that~$|E_{\pi,\alpha}| \leq k$.
nodes.statement_short: A graph has cutwidth $\le k$ if some vertex layout has every cut crossed by at most $k$ edges.
nodes.origin_citation: standard graph-width notion; cf. Cygan et al. 2015
differentia: for each real number $1<\alpha<|V|$ we have that for the \emph{cut} at $\alpha$, defined as~$E_{\pi,\alpha}:=\{ \{u,v\} \in E: \pi(u) < \alpha < \pi(v)\}$, it holds that~$|E_{\pi,\alpha}| \leq k$

nodes.name: Kernelization
nodes.statement: Given a (w.l.o.g.\ binarily encoded) instance $(x,k) \in \{0,1\}^* \times \mathbb{N}$ of some parameterized problem $L$, a \emph{kernelization} for~$L$ produces in polynomial time an instance~$(x',k')$ satisfying: $(x',k') \in L \iff (x,k) \in L$ and $|x'| + k' \leq f(k)$ for some fixed computable function~$f(k)$.
nodes.statement_short: Polynomial-time preprocessing producing an equivalent instance whose total size is bounded by a function of the parameter.
nodes.genus: preprocessing procedure that reduces an instance to its ``computationally hard core"
differentia: $(x',k') \in L \iff (x,k) \in L$ and $|x'| + k' \leq f(k)$ for some fixed computable function~$f(k)$

nodes.name: Turing Machine
nodes.statement: A Turing machine is defined as a tuple $M=(\Sigma, Q, q_0, F, \delta)$, where $\Sigma$ is the alphabet, $Q$ is the set of states, $q_0\in Q$ is the initial state, $F\subseteq Q$ are the accepting states, and~$\delta \subseteq ((\Sigma\cup\{\square\}) \times Q)\times (\Sigma\times Q\times \{-1, 0, 1\})$ is the transition relation, where $\square$ denotes the blank symbol in an empty cell.
nodes.statement_short: Single-tape non-deterministic Turing machine as a 5-tuple of alphabet, states, initial state, accepting states and transition relation.
differentia: $\delta \subseteq ((\Sigma\cup\{\square\}) \times Q)\times (\Sigma\times Q\times \{-1, 0, 1\})$ is the transition relation

nodes.name: Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH)
nodes.statement: The complexity-theoretic assumption we base our results on is the \emph{Exponential Time Hypothesis}, or ETH for short~\cite{ImpagliazzoP01,lokshtanov2011lower}. The Exponential Time Hypothesis states that there is no algorithm for \prob{3-CNF-Sat} running in~$2^{o(n)}$ time, where $n$ denotes the number of variables.
nodes.statement_short: ETH: no $2^{o(n)}$-time algorithm for 3-CNF-Sat on $n$ variables.

nodes.name: Biclique
nodes.statement: \decprob{Biclique} {An undirected bipartite graph $G=(V=A\uplus B,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a vertex set $X\subseteq V$ of $G$ such that $|X\cap A|=|X\cap B|= k$ and all vertices in $X\cap A$ are adjacent with all vertices in $X\cap B$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a bipartite graph contains a balanced complete bipartite subgraph with $k$ vertices on each side.

nodes.name: Clique
nodes.statement: \decprob{Clique} {An undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a vertex set $X\subseteq V$ of $G$ such that $|X|\geq k$ and all vertices in $X$ are pairwise adjacent in $G$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has $k$ pairwise adjacent vertices.

nodes.name: CNF Sat
nodes.statement: \decprob{CNF Sat} {Given a Boolean formula~$\phi$ in conjunctive normal form (CNF).} {Is $\phi$ satisfiable?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide satisfiability of a CNF formula.

nodes.name: Colorful Graph Motif
nodes.statement: \decprob{Colorful Graph Motif} {An undirected graph $G=(V,E)$, an integer $k$, and a vertex coloring function $\col:V \to \{1,\ldots,k\}$.} {Is there a vertex set~$X\subseteq V$ such that $G[X]$ is connected and $X$ contains exactly one vertex of each color?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a $k$-colored graph has a connected subgraph using each color exactly once.

nodes.name: Connected Vertex Cover
nodes.statement: \decprob{Connected Vertex Cover} {An undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a vertex set $X\subseteq V$ in $G$ with $|X|\le k$ and each edge of $G$ is incident to at least one vertex in $X$ and $G[X]$ is connected?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a vertex cover of size $k$ inducing a connected subgraph.

nodes.name: Directed Path
nodes.statement: \decprob{Directed Path} {A directed graph~$G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a simple directed path $P$ of length at least~$k$ in~$G$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a digraph has a simple directed path of length at least $k$.

nodes.name: Hamiltonian Path
nodes.statement: \decprob{Hamiltonian Path} {An undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$.} {Is there a path in $G$ that visits each vertex exactly once?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a path visiting every vertex exactly once.

nodes.name: Hitting Set
nodes.statement: \decprob{Hitting Set} {Given a universe $U$, a family $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U$ of subsets of $U$, and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a subset $U'\subseteq U$ such that $|U'|\leq k$ and $F\cap U'\neq \emptyset$ for all $F\in\mathcal{F}$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether $k$ elements hit every set of a given family.

nodes.name: Independent Set
nodes.statement: \decprob{Independent Set} {An undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a vertex set $X\subseteq V$ of $G$ such that $|X|\geq k$ and $G[X]$ is edge-free?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has $k$ pairwise non-adjacent vertices.

nodes.name: Internal Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: \decprob{Internal Steiner Tree} {An undirected graph $G=(V=N\uplus T,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a subgraph~$H$ of~$G$ such that $H$ is a tree with~$T$ being part of its internal vertices?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a tree subgraph in which all terminals are internal vertices.

nodes.name: $k$-CNF Sat
nodes.statement: \decprob{$k$-CNF Sat} {Given a Boolean formula~$\phi$ in conjunctive normal form (CNF) with at most $k$ literals in each clause.} {Is $\phi$ satisfiable?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide satisfiability of a CNF formula with at most $k$ literals per clause.

nodes.name: Multicolored Path
nodes.statement: \decprob{Multicolored Path} {An undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$ and a vertex coloring function $\col:V \to \{1,\ldots,k\}$.} {Is there a simple path $P$ in $G$ that contains exactly one vertex of each color?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a $k$-colored graph has a simple path using each color exactly once.

nodes.name: Path
nodes.statement: \decprob{Path} {An undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a simple path $P$ of length at least~$k$ in~$G$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a simple path of length at least $k$.

nodes.name: Rooted Path
nodes.statement: \decprob{Rooted Path} {An undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$, an integer~$k$, and a root vertex $r\in V$.} {Is there a simple path $P$ of length at least~$k$ in~$G$ starting at root vertex~$r$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a simple path of length at least $k$ starting at a prescribed root.

nodes.name: Set Cover
nodes.statement: \decprob{Set Cover} {Given a universe $U$, a family of sets $\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^U$, and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a subset $\mathcal{C}\subseteq \mathcal{F}$ such that $|\mathcal{C}|\leq k$ and $U=\bigcup_{C\in \mathcal{C}} C$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether $k$ sets of a family cover the universe.

nodes.name: Short Binary NTM Computation
nodes.statement: \decprob{Short Binary NTM Computation} {Given a single-tape, single-head, non-deterministic Turing machine $M=(\Sigma, Q, q_0, F, \delta)$, where $\Sigma$ is an alphabet of size two, that is $|\Sigma| = 2$, $Q$ is the set of states, $q_0\in Q$ is the initial state, $F\subseteq Q$ are the accepting states, and $\delta \subseteq ((\Sigma\cup\{\square\}) \times Q)\times (\Sigma\times Q\times \{-1, 0, 1\})$ is the transition relation, where $\square$ denotes the blank symbol in an empty cell, a word $x\in\Sigma^*$, and an integer $k$ unary encoding.} {Does $M$ reach an accepting state after $k$ computation steps if the word initially written on the tape is $x$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a binary-alphabet NTM accepts a given word within $k$ steps.

nodes.name: Short NTM Computation
nodes.statement: \decprob{Short NTM Computation} {Given a single-tape, single-head, non-deterministic Turing machine $M=(\Sigma, Q, q_0, F, \delta)$, where $\Sigma$ is the alphabet, $Q$ is the set of states, $q_0\in Q$ is the initial state, $F\subseteq Q$ are the accepting states, and $\delta \subseteq ((\Sigma\cup\{\square\}) \times Q)\times (\Sigma\times Q\times \{-1, 0, 1\})$ is the transition relation, where $\square$ denotes the blank symbol in an empty cell, a word $x\in\Sigma^*$, and an integer $k$ unary encoding.} {Does $M$ reach an accepting state after $k$ computation steps if the word initially written on the tape is $x$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether an NTM accepts a given word within $k$ steps.

nodes.name: Terminal Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: \decprob{Terminal Steiner Tree} {An undirected graph $G=(V=N\uplus T,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a subgraph~$H$ of~$G$ such that $H$ is a tree with~$T$ being its set of leaves?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a tree subgraph whose leaf set is exactly the terminal set.

nodes.name: Vertex Cover
nodes.statement: \decprob{Vertex Cover} {An undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ and an integer~$k$.} {Is there a vertex set $X\subseteq V$ in $G$ with $|X|\le k$ and each edge of $G$ is incident to at least one vertex in $X$?}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a vertex cover of size at most $k$.

nodes.name: Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: given an undirected graph $G=(V=N\uplus T,E)$ ($T$ is called the terminal set) and a positive integer~$k$, decide whether there is a subgraph~$H\subseteq G$ with at most $k+|T|$ vertices such that~$H$ is a tree containing all vertices in~$T$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a tree subgraph on at most $k+|T|$ vertices containing all terminals.

nodes.name: Main Theorem (no strict polynomial kernels)
nodes.statement_short: Unless P=NP, a list of FPT graph, Steiner-tree and short-NTM-computation problems admit no strict polynomial kernel.
assumptions: Unless \PeqNP{}
conclusions: each of the following fixed-parameter tractable problems does not admit a strict polynomial kernel

nodes.name: Diminishability excludes strict polynomial kernels
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}$, for some constant $c$. If $L$ is diminishable and admits a strict polynomial kernel, then \PeqNP{}.
nodes.statement_short: An NP-hard, diminishable problem with a strict polynomial kernel would collapse P and NP.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}$, for some constant $c$.
If $L$ is diminishable and admits a strict polynomial kernel

nodes.name: Diminishability transfers along two-way parameter-non-increasing reductions
nodes.statement: Let~$L_1$ and~$L_2$ be two parameterized problems such that there are parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$. Then we have that~$L_1$ is diminishable if and only if~$L_2$ is diminishable.
nodes.statement_short: Two-way parameter-non-increasing reductions make diminishability equivalent for the two problems.
assumptions: Let~$L_1$ and~$L_2$ be two parameterized problems such that there are parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$.
conclusions: Then we have that~$L_1$ is diminishable if and only if~$L_2$ is diminishable.

nodes.name: Branching plus strict composition yields a parameter diminisher
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. If $L$ admits a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition, then it is diminishable.
nodes.statement_short: Branch-and-compose is a recipe for building parameter diminishers.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem.
If $L$ admits a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition

nodes.name: Non-uniform strict kernels and diminishers imply NP in P/poly
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for some constant $c$. If $L$ is diminishable and admits a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel, then $\NP \subseteq \PTIME/\textnormal{poly}$.
nodes.statement_short: The framework also excludes non-uniform strict polynomial kernels, under $\NP\nsubseteq\PTIME/\text{poly}$.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for some constant $c$.
If $L$ is diminishable and admits a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel

nodes.name: WLOG the constant of a strong diminisher is at least two
nodes.statement: To simplify arguments in the proofs, we assume without loss of generality that the constant of any strong diminisher is at least two for the remainder of this section. Consider a strong parameter diminisher $\calD$ with constant $1<c<2$. Let $\calD'$ be the repetition of $\calD$ exactly $\lceil\log_c 2\rceil$~times. Then~$\calD'$ is a strong parameter diminisher with constant $c':=c^{\lceil\log_c 2\rceil}\geq 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeating a strong diminisher $\lceil\log_c 2\rceil$ times makes its constant at least $2$.

nodes.name: Strong diminishability excludes semi-strict polynomial kernels
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}$, for some constant $c\geq 1$. If $L$ is strongly diminishable and admits a semi-strict polynomial kernel, then \PeqNP{}.
nodes.statement_short: Semi-strict analogue of the main framework theorem: strong diminisher + semi-strict polynomial kernel implies P=NP.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem such that its unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and we have that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}$, for some constant $c\geq 1$.
If $L$ is strongly diminishable and admits a semi-strict polynomial kernel

nodes.name: Set Cover($k\log n$) and Hitting Set($k\log m$) admit no semi-strict polynomial kernel
nodes.statement: Unless \PeqNP{}, \pprob{Set Cover}{k \log n} and \pprob{Hitting Set}{k \log m} does not admit a semi-strict polynomial kernel.
assumptions: Unless \PeqNP{}
conclusions: \pprob{Set Cover}{k \log n} and \pprob{Hitting Set}{k \log m} does not admit a semi-strict polynomial kernel

nodes.name: Problems that are not strongly diminishable under ETH
nodes.statement: Assuming \ETH{}, none of the following problems is strongly diminishable: \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n}, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}, \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\tw}, and \pprob{Clique}{\bw}.
nodes.statement_short: Under ETH, $k$-CNF-Sat($n$), Rooted Path($k$) and Clique parameterized by $\Delta,\tw,\bw$ have no strong diminisher.
assumptions: Assuming \ETH{}
conclusions: none of the following problems is strongly diminishable: \pprob{$k$-CNF-Sat}{n}, \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}, \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\tw}, and \pprob{Clique}{\bw}.

nodes.name: Strong diminishers speed up $2^{O(k)}$ algorithms
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem. If there is an algorithm $\calA$ that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in $2^{O(k)}\cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time and $L$ is strongly diminishable, then there is an algorithm~$\calB$ that solves $L$ in $2^{O(k/ f(x, k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x, k)^{O(1)}}$ time, where $f:L\to \N$ is a function mapping instances of $L$ to the natural numbers with the following property: For every constant $c$ there is a natural number $n$ such that for all instances $(x, k)\in L$ we have that $|x|\ge n$ implies that $f(x, k)\ge c$.
nodes.statement_short: A strong diminisher converts a $2^{O(k)}|x|^{O(1)}$ algorithm into a $2^{O(k/f)}|x|^{f^{O(1)}}$ one.
assumptions: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem.
If there is an algorithm $\calA$ that solves any instance~$(x,k)\in L$ in $2^{O(k)}\cdot |x|^{O(1)}$ time and $L$ is strongly diminishable
conclusions: then there is an algorithm~$\calB$ that solves $L$ in $2^{O(k/ f(x, k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x, k)^{O(1)}}$ time

nodes.name: TST has no polynomial kernel unless NP is in coNP/poly
nodes.statement: We can reduce \pprob{Steiner tree}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} by adding to each terminal a pendant leaf. Set the terminal set in TST to the set of added leaf vertices, and ask for a terminal Steiner tree of size $k'=k+|T|$. This is a polynomial parameter transformation, and hence refutes the existence of a polynomial problem kernel~\cite{DLS14} for TST under \NPnotincoNPslashpoly.
nodes.statement_short: A pendant-leaf polynomial parameter transformation from Steiner Tree rules out polynomial kernels for TST under $\NP\nsubseteq\coNP/\poly$.
assumptions: This is a polynomial parameter transformation
conclusions: refutes the existence of a polynomial problem kernel~\cite{DLS14} for TST under \NPnotincoNPslashpoly

nodes.name: NP in P/poly collapses PH to its second level
nodes.statement: We remark that if $\NP \subseteq \PTIME/\textnormal{poly}$, then the Polynomial Hierarchy collapses to its second level~\cite{karp1982turing} (recall that \NPincoNPslashpoly{} implies a collapse in the Polynomial Hierarchy to its third level).

nodes.name: Parameter diminisher for Rooted Path($k$)
nodes.statement: As an example application of \Cref{lem:branchcomp} above, we consider the parameter diminisher for the \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} problem due to Chen~\emph{et al.}~\cite{chen2011lower}. In this problem we are given an undirected graph~$G=(V,E)$, a distinguished vertex~$r \in V$, and an integer $k$, and our goal is to determine whether there exists a simple path in $G$ of length $k$ that starts at~$r$. Let $v_1,\ldots,v_t$ be the neighbors of~$r$ in $G$. The parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} constructs from $(G,r,k)$ the set of instances~$(G-r,v_1,k-1),\ldots,(G-r,v_t,k-1)$. A strict composition for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k} takes as input the instances $(G_1,r_1,k),\ldots,(G_t,r_t,k)$ and constructs the instance~$(G',r,k+1)$, where~$G'$ is the graph obtained by taking the disjoint union of all $G_i$s and making all their roots adjacent to a new root vertex $r$. Combining these two algorithms gives the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Rooted Path}{k}.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on the root's neighbours (parameter $k-1$), compose by joining all roots to a fresh root (parameter $k+1$).

nodes.name: Diminishability of uncolored and directed Path
nodes.statement: We proved that \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} is diminishable (and thus does not admit a strict polynomial kernel unless \PeqNP{}). Can this result be extended to the uncolored version of the problem? This is also open for the directed case.
nodes.statement_short: Can diminishability of Multicolored Path($k$) be extended to the uncolored and to the directed variants?

nodes.name: Is Connected Vertex Cover($k$) diminishable?
nodes.statement: Is \pprob{Connected Vertex Cover}{k} diminishable?

nodes.name: Is Internal Steiner Tree($k+|T|$) diminishable?
nodes.statement: Is \pprob{Internal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}~\cite{HuangLGH13} diminishable?

nodes.name: Does Clique($\cw$) lack a strong diminisher under ETH?
nodes.statement: \pprob{Clique}{\Delta}, \pprob{Clique}{\tw}, \pprob{Clique}{\bw} do not have strong diminishers under the \ETH{} (\Cref{sec:nodiminishers}). Is this also true for \pprob{Clique}{\cw}?
nodes.statement_short: Clique parameterized by cutwidth is the remaining open case for ETH-based exclusion of strong diminishers.

nodes.name: Is Path($k$) diminishable?
nodes.statement: it remains open whether the problem \pprob{Path}{k}, asking whether a given graph contains a simple path of length $k$, is diminishable

nodes.name: Polynomial kernel but no strict polynomial kernel?

nodes.name: Parameter decrease of the Set Cover strong diminisher
nodes.statement: \[k'\log n' \leq \frac{k+1}{2}\log (n+1) \stackrel{k\geq 2}{\leq} \frac{3k}{4}\log (n+1) \leq \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log ((n+1)^{\sqrt{3}/2}) \stackrel{n\geq 5}{\leq} \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}k\log (n).\]
nodes.statement_short: Chain of inequalities showing $k'\log n' \le (\sqrt{3}/2)\,k\log n$.

nodes.name: Instance-size blow-up under repeated strong diminishing
nodes.statement: \[ |x'| \leq |x|^{b^{\lceil\log_{\cmin} f(x,k)\rceil}} \leq |x|^{b^{2\log_{\cmin} f(x,k)}} \leq |x|^{f(x,k)^{c_3}},\, \text{for some constant $c_3\geq 1$.} \]
nodes.statement_short: The instance size stays bounded by $|x|^{f(x,k)^{c_3}}$.

nodes.name: Parameter decrease under repeated strong diminishing
nodes.statement: \[ k' = k/d^{\lceil\log_{\cmin} f(x,k)\rceil}\leq k/d^{\log_{\cmin} f(x,k)} \leq k/d^{\log_{d} f(x,k)}\leq k/f(x,k) . \]
nodes.statement_short: The parameter drops to at most $k/f(x,k)$.

nodes.name: Resulting running time of algorithm $\calB$
nodes.statement: \[2^{c_1\cdot k'}\cdot |x'|^{c_2} \leq 2^{c_1\cdot k/f(x,k)}\cdot |x|^{c_2\cdot f(x,k)^{c_3}} \in 2^{O(k/ f(x,k))}\cdot |x|^{f(x,k)^{O(1)}}.\qedhere\]
nodes.statement_short: Composite running time $2^{O(k/f)}\cdot|x|^{f^{O(1)}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the diminishability-transfer lemma
nodes.statement: Let~$L_1$ with parameter~$k_1$ and~$L_2$ with parameter~$k_2$ be two parameterized problems. Let~$\calA_1$ and $\calA_2$ be parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$, respectively. Let~$\calD_2$ be a parameter diminisher for~$L_2$. Let $(x_1,k_1)$ be an arbitrary instance of~$L_1$. Apply $\calA_1$ to $(x_1,k_1)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2,k_2)$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2\leq k_1$. Next, apply $\calD_2$ to~$(x_2,k_2)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2',k_2')$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2'<k_2$. Finally, apply $\calA_2$ to $(x_2',k_2')$ to obtain the instance~$(x_1',k_1')$ of~$L_1$ with $k_1'\leq k_2'$. As $k_1'\leq k_2'<k_2 \leq k_1$, the above combination of $\calA_1$, $\calD_2$, and~$\calA_2$ forms a parameter diminisher for~$L_1$. To get the reverse direction, exchange the roles of~$L_1$ and~$L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Chain the two reductions around a diminisher for $L_2$ to obtain one for $L_1$; swap roles for the converse.

nodes.name: Set up the two problems and reductions
nodes.statement: Let~$L_1$ with parameter~$k_1$ and~$L_2$ with parameter~$k_2$ be two parameterized problems. Let~$\calA_1$ and $\calA_2$ be parameter-non-increasing reductions from~$L_1$ to~$L_2$ and from~$L_2$ to~$L_1$, respectively. Let~$\calD_2$ be a parameter diminisher for~$L_2$. Let $(x_1,k_1)$ be an arbitrary instance of~$L_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix the reductions $\calA_1,\calA_2$, a diminisher $\calD_2$ for $L_2$, and an arbitrary $L_1$-instance.

nodes.name: Reduce from $L_1$ to $L_2$
nodes.statement: Apply $\calA_1$ to $(x_1,k_1)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2,k_2)$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2\leq k_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Map the instance into $L_2$ without increasing the parameter.

nodes.name: Diminish inside $L_2$
nodes.statement: Next, apply $\calD_2$ to~$(x_2,k_2)$ to obtain the instance $(x_2',k_2')$ of~$L_2$ with $k_2'<k_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the $L_2$-diminisher to strictly decrease the parameter.

nodes.name: Reduce back to $L_1$
nodes.statement: Finally, apply $\calA_2$ to $(x_2',k_2')$ to obtain the instance~$(x_1',k_1')$ of~$L_1$ with $k_1'\leq k_2'$.
nodes.statement_short: Map back into $L_1$, again without increasing the parameter.

nodes.name: Conclude the parameter strictly decreased
nodes.statement: As $k_1'\leq k_2'<k_2 \leq k_1$, the above combination of $\calA_1$, $\calD_2$, and~$\calA_2$ forms a parameter diminisher for~$L_1$.
nodes.statement_short: The composed chain strictly decreases the parameter, so it is a diminisher for $L_1$.

nodes.name: Symmetry gives the converse
nodes.statement: To get the reverse direction, exchange the roles of~$L_1$ and~$L_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Swap $L_1$ and $L_2$ for the other implication.

nodes.name: Proof of the branch-and-compose lemma
nodes.statement: Let $(x, k)$ be an instance of a parameterized problem $L$ and $c$ be the constant associated with a strict composition for~$L$. We recursively apply the parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$L$ $c+1$ times to produce $t^{c+1}$ instances $(x_i,k^*)$ with $k^* < k-c$, since every time the parameter is decreased at least by one. The strict composition, receiving $t^{c+1}$ instances, produces an instance~$(y, k')$ with~$k'\leq k^*+c<k$ of $L$ which is a yes-instance if and only if $(x, k)$ is a yes-instance. Hence, the whole procedure is a parameter diminisher for~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the branching rule $c+1$ times, then compose once; the additive $+c$ cannot undo the $c+1$ decrease.

nodes.name: Fix instance and composition constant
nodes.statement: Let $(x, k)$ be an instance of a parameterized problem $L$ and $c$ be the constant associated with a strict composition for~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the instance and the strict composition's additive constant $c$.

nodes.name: Branch $c+1$ times
nodes.statement: We recursively apply the parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$L$ $c+1$ times to produce $t^{c+1}$ instances $(x_i,k^*)$ with $k^* < k-c$, since every time the parameter is decreased at least by one.
nodes.statement_short: Recursive branching yields $t^{c+1}$ instances with parameter below $k-c$.

nodes.name: Compose the branches
nodes.statement: The strict composition, receiving $t^{c+1}$ instances, produces an instance~$(y, k')$ with~$k'\leq k^*+c<k$ of $L$ which is a yes-instance if and only if $(x, k)$ is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Compose back into a single equivalent instance with $k'\leq k^*+c<k$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, the whole procedure is a parameter diminisher for~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: The combined procedure is a parameter diminisher.

nodes.name: Proof of the non-uniform variant
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem whose unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and it holds that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for a constant $c\geq 1$. Let $\calD$ be a parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant $c_d\geq 1$ and let $\calA$ be a non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization for~$L$ with constant~$c_a>1$. \iflong{}We show that we can solve any instance $(x,k)$ of $L$, with $k$ being the parameter, in non-uniform polynomial time. \fi{} Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$. Apply $\calD$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil (c_a+1)/c_d\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\calD^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k-c_d \cdot c_r< k-c_a$. Observe that the size of~$|(x', k)|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant. Next, apply $\calA$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq k' + c_a <k$; we explain how to get the advice for $\calA$ in the second half of the proof. Repeating the described procedure at most~$k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in non-uniform polynomial time. In the remainder of the proof, we explain how we obtain the advices for the applications of the non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization. Given any instance size $n$, we claim that for all instances $(x, k) \in L$ with $|(x, k)| = n$, we can upper-bound the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed in the above described procedure by a polynomial in $n$. Let the running time of the diminisher~$\calD$ be $O(n^{c''})$. It follows that~$|(x',k')| \le c_O\cdot n^{c''\cdot c_r}$, where~$(x',k')=\calD^{c_r}(x,k)$ and~$c_O$ is the constant hidden in the $O$-notation. Furthermore, we have that the size of all subsequent instances the diminisher sequence $\calD^{c_r}$ is applied to is smaller than~$k^{c'}$. Thus, the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed can be upper-bounded by $c_O\cdot n^{c' \cdot c''\cdot c_r}$. A list containing all advices for all instance sizes smaller or equal to this bound has polynomial length, since all advices have polynomial length. Hence, the overall procedure can take that list as an advice and use it as a look-up table for the advices needed to apply the non-uniform strict polynomial kernels.
nodes.statement_short: Repeat diminisher-then-kernel to drive the parameter to $1$, and bound the advice list so all needed advices fit in polynomial length.

nodes.name: Hypotheses
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a parameterized problem whose unparameterized version is \NP{}-hard and it holds that $\{(x,k)\in L\mid k\le c\}\in \PTIME{}/\textnormal{poly}$, for a constant $c\geq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Restate the hypotheses on $L$.

nodes.name: Fix diminisher and non-uniform kernelization
nodes.statement: Let $\calD$ be a parameter diminisher for $L$ with constant $c_d\geq 1$ and let $\calA$ be a non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization for~$L$ with constant~$c_a>1$. \iflong{}We show that we can solve any instance $(x,k)$ of $L$, with $k$ being the parameter, in non-uniform polynomial time. \fi{} Let $(x,k)$ be an instance of $L$.
nodes.statement_short: Name the diminisher $\calD$, the non-uniform kernelization $\calA$, and an arbitrary instance.

nodes.name: Apply the diminisher a constant number of times
nodes.statement: Apply $\calD$ on $(x,k)$ exactly $c_r:=\lceil (c_a+1)/c_d\rceil$~times to obtain an equivalent instance $\calD^{c_r}(x,k)=(x',k')$ with $k'\leq k-c_d \cdot c_r< k-c_a$. Observe that the size of~$|(x', k)|$ is still polynomial in $|(x, k)|$ as $c_r$ is a constant.
nodes.statement_short: $c_r$ diminisher applications drop the parameter below $k-c_a$ at polynomial size cost.

nodes.name: Apply the non-uniform kernelization
nodes.statement: Next, apply $\calA$ on $(x',k')$ to obtain an equivalent instance $(x'',k'')$ with $|(x'', k'')|\leq k'^{c'}$, $c'\geq 1$, and $k''\leq k' + c_a <k$; we explain how to get the advice for $\calA$ in the second half of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: One kernelization step yields $k''<k$, deferring the advice question.

nodes.name: Iterate to parameter one
nodes.statement: Repeating the described procedure at most~$k$ times produces an instance $(y,1)$ of $L$, solvable in non-uniform polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: At most $k$ rounds reduce to a trivially solvable instance.

nodes.name: Reduce advice construction to a size bound
nodes.statement: In the remainder of the proof, we explain how we obtain the advices for the applications of the non-uniform strict polynomial kernelization. Given any instance size $n$, we claim that for all instances $(x, k) \in L$ with $|(x, k)| = n$, we can upper-bound the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed in the above described procedure by a polynomial in $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Claim it suffices to polynomially bound the sizes of all instances that need a kernel.

nodes.name: Bound those instance sizes
nodes.statement: Let the running time of the diminisher~$\calD$ be $O(n^{c''})$. It follows that~$|(x',k')| \le c_O\cdot n^{c''\cdot c_r}$, where~$(x',k')=\calD^{c_r}(x,k)$ and~$c_O$ is the constant hidden in the $O$-notation. Furthermore, we have that the size of all subsequent instances the diminisher sequence $\calD^{c_r}$ is applied to is smaller than~$k^{c'}$. Thus, the sizes of all instances $(x^*, k^*)$ for which a non-uniform strict polynomial kernel needs to be computed can be upper-bounded by $c_O\cdot n^{c' \cdot c''\cdot c_r}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose the polynomial size growth of $\calD^{c_r}$ with the kernel bound.

nodes.name: Assemble the advice look-up table
nodes.statement: A list containing all advices for all instance sizes smaller or equal to this bound has polynomial length, since all advices have polynomial length. Hence, the overall procedure can take that list as an advice and use it as a look-up table for the advices needed to apply the non-uniform strict polynomial kernels.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-length list of advices serves the whole procedure.

nodes.name: Proof that Clique($\cw$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: Let $(G=(V, E), \cw(G), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Clique}{\cw}. The following is a parameter-decreasing branching rule for $(G=(V, E),\cw(G),k)$: For each $v \in V$, let $G_v$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ induced by the open neighborhood of $v$, that is, $G_v=G[N(v)]$. It is not difficult to see that~$G$ has a clique of size $k$ if and only if some $G_v$ has a clique of size $k-1$. We next argue that $\cw(G_v) < \cw(G)$ for all $v \in V$. Consider an optimal linear ordering of~$G$, and for any vertex~$v \in V$, consider the ordering restricted to the closed neighborhood of~$v$ in the optimal ordering. By removing~$v$, we remove at least one edge in any cut of the linear ordering, giving us a linear ordering of $G_v$ which has cutwidth smaller than the optimal ordering for $G$. Hence, $\cw(G_v) < \cw(G)$ for each~$v \in V$, and the above algorithm is indeed a parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Clique}{\cw}. For the composition step we take the disjoint union of all graphs. Since a graph has a clique of size $k$ if and only if one of its connected components has a clique of size $k$, and since the cutwidth of a graph $G$ equals the maximum cutwidth of its connected components, this is a strict composition for \pprob{Clique}{\cw}. Applying \Cref{lem:branchcomp}, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on neighbourhoods $G[N(v)]$ (cutwidth strictly drops), compose by disjoint union, then invoke the branch-and-compose lemma.

nodes.name: Fix the instance
nodes.statement: Let $(G=(V, E), \cw(G), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Clique}{\cw}.
nodes.statement_short: Take an arbitrary Clique instance parameterized by cutwidth.

nodes.name: Neighbourhood branching rule
nodes.statement: The following is a parameter-decreasing branching rule for $(G=(V, E),\cw(G),k)$: For each $v \in V$, let $G_v$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ induced by the open neighborhood of $v$, that is, $G_v=G[N(v)]$. It is not difficult to see that~$G$ has a clique of size $k$ if and only if some $G_v$ has a clique of size $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: Branch to the induced neighbourhoods $G_v=G[N(v)]$ with target size $k-1$.

nodes.name: Cutwidth strictly decreases
nodes.statement: We next argue that $\cw(G_v) < \cw(G)$ for all $v \in V$. Consider an optimal linear ordering of~$G$, and for any vertex~$v \in V$, consider the ordering restricted to the closed neighborhood of~$v$ in the optimal ordering. By removing~$v$, we remove at least one edge in any cut of the linear ordering, giving us a linear ordering of $G_v$ which has cutwidth smaller than the optimal ordering for $G$. Hence, $\cw(G_v) < \cw(G)$ for each~$v \in V$, and the above algorithm is indeed a parameter-decreasing branching rule for \pprob{Clique}{\cw}.
nodes.statement_short: Restricting an optimal layout and deleting $v$ removes an edge from every cut.

nodes.name: Disjoint union is a strict composition
nodes.statement: For the composition step we take the disjoint union of all graphs. Since a graph has a clique of size $k$ if and only if one of its connected components has a clique of size $k$, and since the cutwidth of a graph $G$ equals the maximum cutwidth of its connected components, this is a strict composition for \pprob{Clique}{\cw}.
nodes.statement_short: Cliques and cutwidth both localize to connected components, so disjoint union composes strictly.

nodes.name: Invoke the branch-and-compose lemma
nodes.statement: Applying \Cref{lem:branchcomp}, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude via the branch-and-compose lemma.

nodes.name: Proof that Terminal Steiner Tree($k+|T|$) is FPT
nodes.statement: We give an FPT-reduction from \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. As \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} is fixed-parameter tractable~\cite{DreyfusW71}, the claim follows. Let $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ be an instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|}. We construct an equivalent instance~$(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} as follows. Let $G'$ be initially a copy of~$G$. For each~$t\in T$, apply the following. For each edge~$\{v,t\}\in E$, remove~$\{v,t\}$ from~$G'$ and add a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ to~$G'$ with endpoints~$v$ and~$t$. Set~$k'=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k$. This finishes the reduction. Clearly, the construction can be done in FPT-time. We show that $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} if and only if $(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. Let~$H$ be a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$ with $\ell\leq k+|T|$ vertices. We construct a Steiner tree~$H'$ in~$G'$ from~$H$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices as follows. Recall that each~$t\in T$ has exactly one neighbor~$v_t$ in~$H$. Hence, obtain~$H'$ by replacing for each~$t\in T$ the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E(H)$ by the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. It is not difficult to see~$H'$ is a Steiner tree in~$G'$. Moreover, $\ell'=|V(H')|=|V(H)|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq k+|T|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k'+|T|$. Conversely, let~$H'$ be a minimum Steiner tree in~$G'$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices. We state some first observations on~$H'$. Observe that no inner vertex of the paths added in the construction step from~$G$ to~$G'$ is a leaf of~$H'$ (as otherwise~$H'$ is not minimum). Moreover, as~$H'$ contains each~$t\in T$,~$H'$ contains a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ for each~$t\in T$. Suppose that there is a terminal~$t\in T$ such that~$t$ is not a leaf in~$H'$. Then~$H'$ contains at least~$|T|+(|T|+1)\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+2(k+|T|)-1=k'+(k+|T|)-1>k'+|T|$, yielding a contradiction. Hence, each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$. We show how to obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H'$ with at most~$k+|T|$ vertices. As each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$, there is exactly one neighbor~$v_t\in N_G(t)$ such that~$H'$ contains the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. Replace for each~$t\in T$ the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$ in~$H'$ by the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E$ to obtain~$H$ from~$H'$. Note that~$H$ is a terminal Steiner tree. Moreover, $|V(H)|=|V(H')|-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq |T|+|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace every terminal edge by a long path so terminals are forced to be leaves, reducing TST to Steiner Tree.

nodes.name: Reduce to Steiner Tree
nodes.statement: We give an FPT-reduction from \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} to \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}. As \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} is fixed-parameter tractable~\cite{DreyfusW71}, the claim follows.
nodes.statement_short: Set up an FPT-reduction to the FPT problem Steiner Tree.

nodes.name: Construct the reduced instance
nodes.statement: Let $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ be an instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|}. We construct an equivalent instance~$(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|} as follows. Let $G'$ be initially a copy of~$G$. For each~$t\in T$, apply the following. For each edge~$\{v,t\}\in E$, remove~$\{v,t\}$ from~$G'$ and add a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ to~$G'$ with endpoints~$v$ and~$t$. Set~$k'=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k$. This finishes the reduction. Clearly, the construction can be done in FPT-time.
nodes.statement_short: Subdivide every terminal edge into a path of length $2(k+|T|)$ and rescale $k'$.

nodes.name: State the equivalence to be shown
nodes.statement: We show that $(G=(N\uplus T,E),k)$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{TST}{k+|T|} if and only if $(G'=(N'\uplus T,E'),k')$ is a yes-instance of \pprob{Steiner Tree}{k'+|T|}.
nodes.statement_short: Announce the two directions of the correctness proof.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Let~$H$ be a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$ with $\ell\leq k+|T|$ vertices. We construct a Steiner tree~$H'$ in~$G'$ from~$H$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices as follows. Recall that each~$t\in T$ has exactly one neighbor~$v_t$ in~$H$. Hence, obtain~$H'$ by replacing for each~$t\in T$ the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E(H)$ by the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. It is not difficult to see~$H'$ is a Steiner tree in~$G'$. Moreover, $\ell'=|V(H')|=|V(H)|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq k+|T|+|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k'+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand each terminal edge of $H$ into its path to get a Steiner tree of the right size.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, let~$H'$ be a minimum Steiner tree in~$G'$ with $\ell'\leq k'+|T|$ vertices. We state some first observations on~$H'$. Observe that no inner vertex of the paths added in the construction step from~$G$ to~$G'$ is a leaf of~$H'$ (as otherwise~$H'$ is not minimum). Moreover, as~$H'$ contains each~$t\in T$,~$H'$ contains a path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ for each~$t\in T$. Suppose that there is a terminal~$t\in T$ such that~$t$ is not a leaf in~$H'$. Then~$H'$ contains at least~$|T|+(|T|+1)\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)=|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+2(k+|T|)-1=k'+(k+|T|)-1>k'+|T|$, yielding a contradiction. Hence, each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$. We show how to obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H'$ with at most~$k+|T|$ vertices. As each terminal~$t\in T$ forms a leaf in~$H'$, there is exactly one neighbor~$v_t\in N_G(t)$ such that~$H'$ contains the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$. Replace for each~$t\in T$ the path of length~$2(k+|T|)$ connecting~$v_t$ with~$t$ in~$H'$ by the edge~$\{v_t,t\}\in E$ to obtain~$H$ from~$H'$. Note that~$H$ is a terminal Steiner tree. Moreover, $|V(H)|=|V(H')|-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)\leq |T|+|T|\cdot(2(k+|T|)-1)+k-|T|(2(k+|T|)-1)=k+|T|$.
nodes.statement_short: A counting argument forces every terminal to be a leaf; contract the paths back to edges.

nodes.name: Proof that Terminal Steiner Tree($k+|T|$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Together with~\Cref{lem:branchcomp}, the claim then follows. Let~$(G=(N\uplus T,E), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|} (we can assume that $G$ has a connected component containing~$T$). We make several assumptions first. We can assume that~$|T|\geq 3$ (otherwise a shortest path is the optimal solution) and additionally that for all terminals $t\in T$ it holds that~$N_G(t)\not\subseteq T$ (as otherwise the instance is a no-instance). Moreover, we can assume that there is no vertex~$v\in N$ such that $T\subseteq N_G(v)$, as otherwise we immediately output whether $k\geq 1$. Select a terminal $t^*\in T$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ denote the neighbors of~$t^*$ in~$G-(T\setminus\{t^*\})$. We create $d$ instances $(G_1,k-1),\ldots,(G_d,k-1)$ as follows. Define~$G_i$, $i\in[d]$, by $G_i:=G-v_i$. Turn the vertices in~$N_G(v_i)$ in~$G_i$ into a clique, that is, for each distinct vertices $v,w\in N_G(v_i)$ add the edge~$\{v,w\}$ if not yet present. This finishes the construction of~$G_i$. It is not hard to see that the construction can be done in polynomial time. We show that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ if and only if there is an~$i\in[d]$ such that~$G_i$ admits a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k-1+|T|$. Suppose that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ of size~$k+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H$, there is exactly one neighbor $v_i$, $i\in[d]$, being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H$. Let~$w$ be a neighbor of~$v_i$ in~$H-T$ and let $A:=N_H(v_i)$ (note that~$t^*\in A$). Then~$H_i$ forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G_i$, where~$H_i$ is the tree obtained from~$H$ by deleting~$v_i$ and connecting~$w$ with all vertices in~$A$. Moreover, $H_i$ is of size~$k-1+|T|$. Conversely, let $G_i$ admit a terminal Steiner tree~$H_i$ of size~$k-1+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H_i$, there is exactly one vertex~$w$ being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H_i$. We obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H_i$ as follows. If every edge in~$H_i$ is also present in~$G$, then~$H:=H_i$ also forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$. Otherwise, there is an inclusion-wise maximal edge set~$E'\subseteq E(H_i)$ such that $E'\cap E(G)=\emptyset$. Observe that by construction, the set of endpoints of~$E'$ forms a subset of~$N_G(v_i)$. Let initially~$H$ be a copy of~$H_i$. Delete from~$H$ all edges in~$E'$, add vertex~$v_i$ to~$H$, and for each~$\{x,y\}\in E'$, add the edges~$\{x,v_i\}$ and~$\{y,v_i\}$. Note that~$H$ remains connected after this step, and the set of leaves remains unchanged. Finally, compute a minimum feedback edge set in~$H$ if necessary. Observe that since~$V(H)=V(H_i)\cup\{v_i\}$, $H$ forms a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ in~$G$. Next, we describe the strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Given the instances $(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$, we create an instance $(G',k)$ as follows. Let~$G'$ be initially the disjoint union of~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$. For each $t\in T$, identify its copies in~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$, say~$t_1,\ldots,t_d$, with one vertex~$t'$ corresponding to~$t$. This finishes the construction of~$G'$. Note that for every $i,j\in[d]$, $i\neq j$, any path between a vertex in~$G_i$ and a vertex in $G_j$ contains a terminal vertex. Hence, any terminal Steiner tree in $G'$ contains non-terminal vertices only in~$G_i$ for exactly one~$i\in[d]$. It is not difficult to see that $(G',k)$ is a yes-instance if and only if one of the instances~$(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$ is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Branch on the neighbour of a chosen terminal (deleting it and cliquifying its neighbourhood), compose by identifying terminal copies.

nodes.name: Plan and fix the instance
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Together with~\Cref{lem:branchcomp}, the claim then follows. Let~$(G=(N\uplus T,E), k)$ be an instance of \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|} (we can assume that $G$ has a connected component containing~$T$).

nodes.statement: We make several assumptions first. nodes.name: Branching construction
nodes.statement: Select a terminal $t^*\in T$, and let $v_1,\ldots,v_d$ denote the neighbors of~$t^*$ in~$G-(T\setminus\{t^*\})$. We create $d$ instances $(G_1,k-1),\ldots,(G_d,k-1)$ as follows. nodes.statement: We show that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ if and only if there is an~$i\in[d]$ such that~$G_i$ admits a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k-1+|T|$.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Suppose that~$G$ has a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ of size~$k+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H$, there is exactly one neighbor $v_i$, $i\in[d]$, being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H$. Then~$H_i$ forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G_i$, where~$H_i$ is the tree obtained from~$H$ by deleting~$v_i$ and connecting~$w$ with all vertices in~$A$. Moreover, $H_i$ is of size~$k-1+|T|$.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, let $G_i$ admit a terminal Steiner tree~$H_i$ of size~$k-1+|T|$. As~$t^*$ is a leaf in~$H_i$, there is exactly one vertex~$w$ being the neighbor of~$t^*$ in~$H_i$. We obtain a terminal Steiner tree~$H$ in~$G$ from~$H_i$ as follows. If every edge in~$H_i$ is also present in~$G$, then~$H:=H_i$ also forms a terminal Steiner tree in~$G$. Otherwise, there is an inclusion-wise maximal edge set~$E'\subseteq E(H_i)$ such that $E'\cap E(G)=\emptyset$. Observe that by construction, the set of endpoints of~$E'$ forms a subset of~$N_G(v_i)$. Let initially~$H$ be a copy of~$H_i$. Delete from~$H$ all edges in~$E'$, add vertex~$v_i$ to~$H$, and for each~$\{x,y\}\in E'$, add the edges~$\{x,v_i\}$ and~$\{y,v_i\}$. Note that~$H$ remains connected after this step, and the set of leaves remains unchanged. Finally, compute a minimum feedback edge set in~$H$ if necessary. Observe that since~$V(H)=V(H_i)\cup\{v_i\}$, $H$ forms a terminal Steiner tree of size~$k+|T|$ in~$G$.
nodes.statement_short: Re-insert $v_i$ to replace the added clique edges and clean up cycles.

nodes.name: Strict composition
nodes.statement: Next, we describe the strict composition for \pprob{Terminal Steiner Tree}{k+|T|}. Given the instances $(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$, we create an instance $(G',k)$ as follows. Let~$G'$ be initially the disjoint union of~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$. For each $t\in T$, identify its copies in~$G_1,\ldots,G_d$, say~$t_1,\ldots,t_d$, with one vertex~$t'$ corresponding to~$t$. This finishes the construction of~$G'$. Note that for every $i,j\in[d]$, $i\neq j$, any path between a vertex in~$G_i$ and a vertex in $G_j$ contains a terminal vertex. Hence, any terminal Steiner tree in $G'$ contains non-terminal vertices only in~$G_i$ for exactly one~$i\in[d]$. It is not difficult to see that $(G',k)$ is a yes-instance if and only if one of the instances~$(G_1,k),\ldots,(G_d,k)$ is a yes-instance.
nodes.statement_short: Take the disjoint union and identify the copies of each terminal into one vertex.

nodes.name: Proof that Multicolored Path($k$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k}. The result will then follow directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}. Let $(G=(V,E),\col)$ be an instance of the \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} problem. The parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$(G=(V,E),\col)$ creates a graph $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ for each ordered triplet $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vertices of~$V$ such that $v_1,v_2,v_3$ is a multicolored path in $G$. The graph~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ is constructed from $G$ as follows: We delete from $G$ all vertices $w\in V\setminus\{v_2,v_3\}$ with~$\col(w)\in\{\col(v_1),\col(v_2),\col(v_3)\}$. Following this, only vertices of $k-1$ colors remain, and $v_2$ and~$v_3$ are the only vertices colored $\col(v_2)$ and $\col(v_3)$, respectively. We then delete all edges incident with~$v_2$, apart from $\{v_2,v_3\}$, and relabel all colors so that the image of $\col$ for~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ is~$\{1,\ldots,k-1\}$. Clearly our parameter decreasing branching rule can be performed in polynomial time. Furthermore, the parameter decreases in each output instance. We show that the first requirement of Definition~\ref{def:branching} holds as well: Indeed, suppose that $G$ has a multicolored path~$v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ of length~$k$. Then $v_2,\ldots,v_k$ is a multicolored path of length~$k-1$ in~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ by construction. Conversely, suppose there is a multicolored path $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ of length $k-1$ in some $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$. Then since $v_2$ is the only vertex of color $\col(v_2)$ in $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$, and since $v_2$ is only adjacent to~$v_3$, it must be w.l.o.g.\ that $u_2=v_2$ and $u_3=v_3$. Therefore, since $v_1$ is adjacent to $v_2$ in $G$, and no vertices of $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ have color $\col(v_1)$ in $G$, the sequence of $v_1,u_2,\ldots,u_k$ forms a multicolored path of length $k$ in~$G$. The strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} is as follows. Given a sequence of inputs~$(G_1,\col_1),\ldots,(G_t,\col_t)$, the strict composition constructs the disjoint union $G$ and the coloring function~$\col$ of all graphs $G_i$ and coloring functions $\col_i$, $1\leq i\leq t$. Clearly, $(G,\col)$ contains a multicolored path of length $k$ if and only if there is a multicolored path of length $k$ in some~$(G_i,\col_i)$. The result thus follows directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}.
nodes.statement_short: Branch over multicolored triples $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, deleting their colors and isolating $v_2$; compose by disjoint union.

nodes.name: Plan and fix the instance
nodes.statement: We present a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k}. The result will then follow directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}. Let $(G=(V,E),\col)$ be an instance of the \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} problem.

nodes.name: Triple-branching construction
nodes.statement: The parameter-decreasing branching rule for~$(G=(V,E),\col)$ creates a graph $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ for each ordered triplet $(v_1,v_2,v_3)$ of vertices of~$V$ such that $v_1,v_2,v_3$ is a multicolored path in $G$. We then delete all edges incident with~$v_2$, apart from $\{v_2,v_3\}$, and relabel all colors so that the image of $\col$ for~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ is~$\{1,\ldots,k-1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For each multicolored triple, delete its three color classes (except $v_2,v_3$) and isolate $v_2$ to $v_3$.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Clearly our parameter decreasing branching rule can be performed in polynomial time. Furthermore, the parameter decreases in each output instance. We show that the first requirement of Definition~\ref{def:branching} holds as well: Indeed, suppose that $G$ has a multicolored path~$v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_k$ of length~$k$. Then $v_2,\ldots,v_k$ is a multicolored path of length~$k-1$ in~$G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$ by construction.
nodes.statement_short: A length-$k$ multicolored path yields a length-$(k-1)$ one after dropping its first vertex.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose there is a multicolored path $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ of length $k-1$ in some $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$. Then since $v_2$ is the only vertex of color $\col(v_2)$ in $G_{(v_1,v_2,v_3)}$, and since $v_2$ is only adjacent to~$v_3$, it must be w.l.o.g.\ that $u_2=v_2$ and $u_3=v_3$. Therefore, since $v_1$ is adjacent to $v_2$ in $G$, and no vertices of $u_2,\ldots,u_k$ have color $\col(v_1)$ in $G$, the sequence of $v_1,u_2,\ldots,u_k$ forms a multicolored path of length $k$ in~$G$.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of $v_2$'s color and its single edge force the path to be extendable by $v_1$.

nodes.name: Strict composition and conclusion
nodes.statement: The strict composition for \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} is as follows. Given a sequence of inputs~$(G_1,\col_1),\ldots,(G_t,\col_t)$, the strict composition constructs the disjoint union $G$ and the coloring function~$\col$ of all graphs $G_i$ and coloring functions $\col_i$, $1\leq i\leq t$. Clearly, $(G,\col)$ contains a multicolored path of length $k$ if and only if there is a multicolored path of length $k$ in some~$(G_i,\col_i)$. The result thus follows directly from \Cref{lem:branchcomp}.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint union of the graphs and colorings composes; conclude by the branch-and-compose lemma.

nodes.name: Proof for Multicolored Path($k\log n$)
nodes.statement: Chen, Flum, and M\"{u}ller~\cite[Prop.~3.10]{chen2011lower} proved that if $L$ is a parameterized problem which can be solved in $2^{k^{O(1)}}|x|^{O(1)}$ time, where $k$ is the parameter and $|x|$ is the instance size, then $L(k)$ has a polynomial kernel if and only if $L(k \log |x|)$ has a polynomial kernel. It is easy to verify that their proof also holds for strict polynomial kernels. Thus, as \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} can be solved in $2^{k^{O(1)}}n^{O(1)}$~\cite{AlonYZ95}, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Transfer Chen et al.'s $k$ vs.\ $k\log|x|$ kernel-equivalence to strict kernels.

nodes.name: Recall the transfer proposition
nodes.statement: Chen, Flum, and M\"{u}ller~\cite[Prop.~3.10]{chen2011lower} proved that if $L$ is a parameterized problem which can be solved in $2^{k^{O(1)}}|x|^{O(1)}$ time, where $k$ is the parameter and $|x|$ is the instance size, then $L(k)$ has a polynomial kernel if and only if $L(k \log |x|)$ has a polynomial kernel.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the $k$ versus $k\log|x|$ kernel-equivalence for $2^{k^{O(1)}}|x|^{O(1)}$-solvable problems.

nodes.name: Observe it holds for strict kernels
nodes.statement: It is easy to verify that their proof also holds for strict polynomial kernels.
nodes.statement_short: The same argument goes through verbatim for strict kernels.

nodes.name: Apply to Multicolored Path
nodes.statement: Thus, as \pprob{Multicolored Path}{k} can be solved in $2^{k^{O(1)}}n^{O(1)}$~\cite{AlonYZ95}, the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Multicolored Path meets the running-time hypothesis, so the result transfers.

nodes.name: Proof that Colorful Graph Motif($k$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: We show that there is a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Let $(G=(V,E),\col)$ be an instance of \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Assume there are only edges between differently colored vertices. For each~$\{v, w\} \in E$, the parameter-decreasing branching rule creates a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ which is a copy of~$G$ where all vertices of colors $\col(v)$ and $\col(w)$ are removed. Furthermore, a new vertex $v^\star$ is added with color $\col(v^\star) = \col(v)$ and with edges to all vertices in~$N(v)\cup N(w)$ that have not been removed. Clearly,~$G_{\{v, w\}}$ only contains vertices of $k-1$ different colors and is computable in polynomial time. Also, if $G$ contains a colorful motif~$\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ where, without loss of generality, $\{v_1, v_2\} \in E$, then $G_{\{v_1, v_2\}}$ contains the colorful motif~$\{v^\star, v_3, \ldots, v_k\}$. Conversely, if a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ contains a colorful motif, then it has to contain~$v^\star$ since it is the only vertex of its color. Let $\{v^\star, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ be a colorful motif in $G_{\{v, w\}}$, then $\{v, w, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ is a colorful motif in $G$ since $v^\star$ is connected to some vertex $v_i$ in the motif and hence, by construction, $v_i$ is connected to $v$ or to $w$ and there is an edge between $v$ and $w$. The strict composition constructs the disjoint union of the sequence of inputs. Clearly, the disjoint union has a colorful motif if and only if one of the input graphs has a colorful motif. \Cref{lem:branchcomp} now yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Branch over edges $\{v,w\}$, merging their two color classes into one new vertex $v^\star$; compose by disjoint union.

nodes.name: Plan and fix the instance
nodes.statement: We show that there is a parameter-decreasing branching rule and a strict composition for \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Let $(G=(V,E),\col)$ be an instance of \pprob{Colorful Graph Motif}{k}. Assume there are only edges between differently colored vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Announce branch-and-compose and normalize to properly colored edges.

nodes.name: Edge-branching construction
nodes.statement: For each~$\{v, w\} \in E$, the parameter-decreasing branching rule creates a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ which is a copy of~$G$ where all vertices of colors $\col(v)$ and $\col(w)$ are removed. Clearly,~$G_{\{v, w\}}$ only contains vertices of $k-1$ different colors and is computable in polynomial time.
nodes.statement_short: Contract the pair $\{v,w\}$ into a fresh vertex $v^\star$ after deleting both color classes.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: Also, if $G$ contains a colorful motif~$\{v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ where, without loss of generality, $\{v_1, v_2\} \in E$, then $G_{\{v_1, v_2\}}$ contains the colorful motif~$\{v^\star, v_3, \ldots, v_k\}$.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, if a graph $G_{\{v, w\}}$ contains a colorful motif, then it has to contain~$v^\star$ since it is the only vertex of its color. Let $\{v^\star, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ be a colorful motif in $G_{\{v, w\}}$, then $\{v, w, v_2, \ldots, v_k\}$ is a colorful motif in $G$ since $v^\star$ is connected to some vertex $v_i$ in the motif and hence, by construction, $v_i$ is connected to $v$ or to $w$ and there is an edge between $v$ and $w$.
nodes.statement_short: Expanding $v^\star$ back to $v,w$ keeps the motif connected.

nodes.name: Strict composition and conclusion
nodes.statement: The strict composition constructs the disjoint union of the sequence of inputs. Clearly, the disjoint union has a colorful motif if and only if one of the input graphs has a colorful motif. \Cref{lem:branchcomp} now yields the result.
nodes.statement_short: Disjoint union composes; conclude by the branch-and-compose lemma.

nodes.name: Proof that Short NTM Computation($k+|\Sigma|$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: The main idea behind the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|\Sigma|} is to transform the given Turing machine $M$ to a Turing machine $M'=(\Sigma,Q',q'_0,F',\delta')$ that computes the last two steps of $M$, that is step $k-1$ and step $k$, in one step. (If $k=1$, then the parameter diminisher can produce a trivial \YES{}- or \NO-instance.) To do that, we need to encode the letter and its position on the tape that will be read by Turing machine~$M$ in step $k$ in the states of Turing machine $M'$. Additionally, we need to use the states to count the steps in order to allow the Turing machine $M'$ to recognize when it has to compute two steps of $M$ in one step, and we need to encode the position of the tape which the head is currently looking at. Let $x\in \Sigma^*$ denote the input string, that is initially written on the tape, starting at cell $0$. Note that in $k$ steps, the head of the Turing machine can potentially only move to and read from cells $-k, -k+1, \ldots, 0, \ldots, k-1, k$, assuming the initial head position is $0$. Hence, we set $$Q' = \{q_0'\}\cup (Q\times (\Sigma\cup \{\square\})\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{1,\dots,k-1\})\cup \{\bar{q}\}.$$ So every state different from $q_0'$ and $\bar{q}$ is a tuple consisting of five elements: the state of Turing machine $M$ it corresponds to, the letter that is on a specific position of the tape, that position, the current position of the head, and the current computation step. Every of those states is accepting, it the corresponding state of $M$ is accepting, $q_0'$ is accepting if $q_0$ is accepting, and $\bar{q}$ is not an accepting state. For every transition in $\delta$ from the initial state $q_0$ to some state $q$ we create transitions in~$\delta'$ from the new initial state $q_0'$ to all states $(q,x_i, i, m, 1)$ such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item for $1\le i \le |x|$, $x_i$ is the $i$-th letter of input $x$, for $i=0$, $x_0$ is the letter written by $\delta$ to cell~$0$, and $\square$ otherwise, and \item $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$. \end{compactitem} The following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head. For every transition from a state $q$ to a state $q'$ in $\delta$, we create transitions from states~$(q, x, i, j, t)$ to states $(q', x', i, j', t+1)$ in $\delta'$, such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item $x'=x$ unless we have that $i=j$, in this case the Turing machine writes symbol $y$ into cell $i$ in that transition $\delta$, and hence $x' = y$, \item $j' = j+m$, where $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, and \item $1\le t \le k-3$. \end{compactitem} Again, the following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head. Finally, for every state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ we create a transition in $\delta'$ that on reading symbol $y$ goes to state $(q', x', i, j', k-1)$ without moving the head if the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item There is a transition from $q$ on reading symbol $y$ to a state $q^\star$ in $\delta$ with head movement~$m$ such that $j+m=i$, and \item there is a transition in $\delta$ that, if $M$ is in state $q^\star$ and reads $x$, goes to state $q'$. \end{compactitem} Otherwise, we create a transition in $\delta'$ that goes from state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ and reading symbol $y$ to state $\bar{q}$ without moving the head. No writing is necessary. Turing machine $M'$ needs to non-deterministically guess the position of the head of Turing machine $M$ in step $k-1$ and then simulates the behavior of $M$ until step $k-2$. If the guess was wrong, then $M$ will transition to $\bar{q}$, a non-accepting state. If the guess was correct, then $M'$ accepts in $k-1$ steps if and only if $M$ accepts in $k$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Build $M'$ that guesses the cell read at step $k$ and folds the last two steps of $M$ into one, decreasing $k$ by one at unchanged alphabet.

nodes.name: Idea and encoding requirements
nodes.statement: The main idea behind the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|\Sigma|} is to transform the given Turing machine $M$ to a Turing machine $M'=(\Sigma,Q',q'_0,F',\delta')$ that computes the last two steps of $M$, that is step $k-1$ and step $k$, in one step. (If $k=1$, then the parameter diminisher can produce a trivial \YES{}- or \NO-instance.) To do that, we need to encode the letter and its position on the tape that will be read by Turing machine~$M$ in step $k$ in the states of Turing machine $M'$. Additionally, we need to use the states to count the steps in order to allow the Turing machine $M'$ to recognize when it has to compute two steps of $M$ in one step, and we need to encode the position of the tape which the head is currently looking at. Let $x\in \Sigma^*$ denote the input string, that is initially written on the tape, starting at cell $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Fold steps $k-1$ and $k$ of $M$ into one step of $M'$ by storing the guessed letter, its cell, the head cell and a step counter in the state.

nodes.name: Define the new state set
nodes.statement: Note that in $k$ steps, the head of the Turing machine can potentially only move to and read from cells $-k, -k+1, \ldots, 0, \ldots, k-1, k$, assuming the initial head position is $0$. Hence, we set $$Q' = \{q_0'\}\cup (Q\times (\Sigma\cup \{\square\})\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{-k,\dots,k\}\times\{1,\dots,k-1\})\cup \{\bar{q}\}.$$ So every state different from $q_0'$ and $\bar{q}$ is a tuple consisting of five elements: the state of Turing machine $M$ it corresponds to, the letter that is on a specific position of the tape, that position, the current position of the head, and the current computation step. Every of those states is accepting, it the corresponding state of $M$ is accepting, $q_0'$ is accepting if $q_0$ is accepting, and $\bar{q}$ is not an accepting state.
nodes.statement_short: States of $M'$ are 5-tuples plus a fresh initial state $q_0'$ and a rejecting sink $\bar{q}$.

nodes.name: Transitions out of the initial state
nodes.statement: For every transition in $\delta$ from the initial state $q_0$ to some state $q$ we create transitions in~$\delta'$ from the new initial state $q_0'$ to all states $(q,x_i, i, m, 1)$ such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item for $1\le i \le |x|$, $x_i$ is the $i$-th letter of input $x$, for $i=0$, $x_0$ is the letter written by $\delta$ to cell~$0$, and $\square$ otherwise, and \item $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$. \end{compactitem} The following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head.
nodes.statement_short: From $q_0'$, guess the cell $i$ and its letter $x_i$ while mimicking $M$'s first transition.

nodes.name: Generic transitions
nodes.statement: For every transition from a state $q$ to a state $q'$ in $\delta$, we create transitions from states~$(q, x, i, j, t)$ to states $(q', x', i, j', t+1)$ in $\delta'$, such that the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item $-k\leq i\leq k$, \item $x'=x$ unless we have that $i=j$, in this case the Turing machine writes symbol $y$ into cell $i$ in that transition $\delta$, and hence $x' = y$, \item $j' = j+m$, where $m$ is the movement of the head in the transition $\delta$, that is, $m\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, and \item $1\le t \le k-3$. \end{compactitem} Again, the following stays unchanged in the transition: the letter that needs to be read by the head for the transition to be possible, the letter written to the tape, and the movement of the head.
nodes.statement_short: For steps $1\le t\le k-3$, $M'$ simulates $M$ while updating the tracked cell content, head position and counter.

nodes.name: The merged final transition
nodes.statement: Finally, for every state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ we create a transition in $\delta'$ that on reading symbol $y$ goes to state $(q', x', i, j', k-1)$ without moving the head if the following conditions are met. \begin{compactitem} \item There is a transition from $q$ on reading symbol $y$ to a state $q^\star$ in $\delta$ with head movement~$m$ such that $j+m=i$, and \item there is a transition in $\delta$ that, if $M$ is in state $q^\star$ and reads $x$, goes to state $q'$. \end{compactitem} Otherwise, we create a transition in $\delta'$ that goes from state $(q, x, i, j, k-2)$ and reading symbol $y$ to state $\bar{q}$ without moving the head. No writing is necessary.
nodes.statement_short: At counter $k-2$, execute two $M$-steps at once if the guess is consistent, else fall into $\bar{q}$.

nodes.name: Correctness of the simulation
nodes.statement: Turing machine $M'$ needs to non-deterministically guess the position of the head of Turing machine $M$ in step $k-1$ and then simulates the behavior of $M$ until step $k-2$. If the guess was wrong, then $M$ will transition to $\bar{q}$, a non-accepting state. If the guess was correct, then $M'$ accepts in $k-1$ steps if and only if $M$ accepts in $k$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Wrong guesses reject, correct guesses give acceptance in $k-1$ steps.

nodes.name: Proof that Short NTM Computation($k+|Q|$) is diminishable
nodes.statement: The idea behind the parameter diminisher for \pprob{Short NTM Computation}{k+|Q|} is to merge the symbols on the tape at positions $-1,0,+1$ into a single new symbol. In this way we can produce a Turing machine $M'$ that computes the first two steps of the given Turing machine~$M$ with a single step. (If $k=1$, then the parameter diminisher can produce a trivial \YES{}- or \NO-instance.) More specifically, given a Turing machine $M=(\Sigma, Q, q_0, F, \delta)$, a word $x\in\Sigma^*$, and a positive integer $k$, we construct a Turing machine $M'=(\Sigma',Q,q_0,F,\delta')$ and a word $x'\in\Sigma'^*$ such that~$(M',x',k-1)$ is a \YES{}-instance if and only if $(M,x,k)$ is a \YES{}-instance. We set~$\Sigma'=\Sigma\cup\left((\Sigma\cup\{\square\})\times\Sigma^2\times\{-1,0,+1,S\}\right)$. The set $\{-1,0,+1,S\}$ encodes the position of the head of $M$ when reading a symbol at positions $-1,0,+1$, while $S$ encodes that this is the first step, and hence that we need to compute two steps of $M$ at once. The new input $x'$ is set to~$x'=(\square,x_0,x_1,S) x_2 \dots x_n$, where $x_0\dots x_n=x$. The transition relation $\delta'$ is defined as follows. On symbols in $\Sigma$ the Turing machine~$M'$ behaves like $M$, while on symbols $(\sigma_{-1},\sigma_{0},\sigma_{+1},i)$ with $i\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, we simulate the original Turing machine $M$ on the character $\sigma_i$. If the Turing machine~$M$ moves left or right within~$\{-1,0,1\}$, then we keep the head on the same position and update the value of~$i$. If we move outside the range $\{-1,0,+1\}$, then we move the head to the left and right accordingly. Note that when the Turing machine~$M'$ returns to this symbol, then the value of $i$ will be automatically correct. Finally, on symbols $(\sigma_{-1},\sigma_{0},\sigma_{+1},S)$ we are in state $q_0$ and simulate the first two steps of the Turing machine $M$. Also, we replace $S$ according to the movement of the head. This guarantees that $M'$ will only read such a symbol in the very first step and hence computes two steps of $M$ in one step exactly once. It is not difficult to see that $M'$ accepts $x'$ in $k-1$ steps if and only if $M$ accepts $x$ in $k$ steps.
nodes.statement_short: Enlarge the alphabet (keeping $Q$ fixed) by packing cells $-1,0,+1$ into one symbol so the first two steps of $M$ collapse into one.

nodes.name: Idea: merge three tape cells

nodes.name: Define the transition relation
nodes.statement: The transition relation $\delta'$ is defined as follows. On symbols in $\Sigma$ the Turing machine~$M'$ behaves like $M$, while on symbols $(\sigma_{-1},\sigma_{0},\sigma_{+1},i)$ with $i\in\{-1, 0, 1\}$, we simulate the original Turing machine $M$ on the character $\sigma_i$.
